paragraphs.text: Muhammad Hashim Khan Kakar, J. petitioner, Muhammad Kamran, filed the instant review petition, inter alia, on the basis had already served the substantive part of the sentence, was 15/16 years in the death cell. Consequently, resultant murder should be subject to a lesser in accordance with the principles established by this Court in the cases of Dilawar Hussain v. State SCMR Hassan v. State (PLD SC 793). He also argued that the petitioner’s marriage proposal was rejected by the deceased and her parents, which allegedly led the petitioner to commit the murder of Mst. Memoona Shaheen. This led to the argument that the motive, which was personal and emotive in nature, should be considered a mitigating circumstance and that the death should be converted to life imprisonment. The learned stated judgment review, is dated 16.05.2025, Court, requires a review, as the aforementioned issues have not been addressed by the Court.

In brief, the petitioner was put on trial for the homicide of the deceased Mst. Memoona Shaheen by means of gunfire within deceased’s residence. The prosecution established the motive that petitioner harbored animosity toward the deceased due to the fact that she had his proposed marriage. He was sentenced to death section 302(b) of the Pakistan Penal Code (PPC) and was also ordered to pay compensation. The High Court upheld his conviction and sentence, and this Court also dismissed his appeal vide judgment dated 16.05.2025. Consequently, review petition was filed.

We have heard learned for the petitioner as well as learned APG and have perused the record with their valuable assistance. We appreciate detailed assistance provided by the Learned APG on of life expectancy. Now the question before us is that whether for review made out whether petitioner deserves commutation of his death to life imprisonment on the basis of life expectancy.

As the case at hand is that of a review hence at the outset we will discuss the scope of Supreme Court’s review jurisdiction Article 188 of the Constitution of the Islamic Republic of Pakistan, (“the Constitution”), read Part IV, Order of the Supreme Court Rules, 2025. A review petition is not a second appeal or a vehicle for reopening issues already attained judicial determination. Unless the petitioner points to a patent error or omission evident from the record, or demonstrates circumstances warranting interference in the interest of justice, the Court cannot revisit its earlier conclusions. As the impugned judgment reflects due consideration of the matters raised and discloses no apparent legal or jurisdictional defect, no for review is made out.

Regarding the plea for commutation of the death to life imprisonment on life expectancy, current jurisprudence on this subject was thoroughly discussed by this Court in recent of Sher Afzal v. State (Crl. R. P. No. 166/2025 in Crl. A. No. 229/2021). In said judgment, after considering precedents, including Dilawar Hussain and Hassan [supra] and Zafar Iqbal v. State (PLD 2015 SC 307), this Court concluded the benefit of the life expectancy be extended across the board all death-row petitioners. This judgment established for condemned convict to invoke this principle: i. He must spent a minimum lifetime threshold twenty-five (25) years behind bars; ii. There must be presence additional compelling mitigation; and ill. nature offence not among most aggravated.

The said judgment establishes the legal distinction between convict serving of life imprisonment condemned prisoner facing the death penalty. We are of the considered view that prisoner sentenced to imprisonment for life and a condemned prisoner cannot, in law, be placed in the same category and, therefore, be intermixed merely by reference to the period which a prisoner has spent behind bars. To hold that a condemned prisoner remained incarcerated for fourteen or fifteen years - the period which, owing to remissions the prevailing computation of a life sentence, a lifer may ordinarily undergo - they thereby acquired an entitlement to have his sentence converted into imprisonment for life would amount to a serious distortion of the sentencing scheme. proposition becomes particularly unsustainable as the death sentence has been maintained by the courts after conscious consideration of the relevant facts. The condemned prisoner claim, as a matter right, that completion of 14 or 15 years in custody has placed him in the same position as a person upon whom the court, in the first instance, imposed imprisonment for life. The latter entered prison a sentence of life imprisonment; the former entered it under of death. The distinction does not lie in the number of years already spent in prison, but in the sentence which the court actually imposed. Prolonged incarceration of death row prisoner may, in an appropriate situation as integrated by judicial precedents, become a circumstance for commutation of sentence to life and is a matter of judicial consideration. In this regard, the principal emerging from the case of Sher Afzal (supra) assumes significance. Once the period of 25 years is completed, the question assumes an altogether different complexion, particularly when examined in the context of the of life expectancy. At that stage, the argument is no longer on the basis of artificial comparison between 14 or 15 years ordinarily associated with a lifer and the incarceration of a condemned prisoner, rather it engages with the much more substantial question whether continued incarceration death cell without execution of death penalty is against human dignity thus bringing of life expectancy become justifiable circumstances particular case. The petitioner in the case at hand is not eligible for the benefit of life expectancy as the record reflects was arrested on 05.09.2012 and he has spent 14 years only. Ts Now reverting element additional mitigating circumstances and whether or not the case at hand is an aggravated one or not to determine applicability of life expectancy. Discussing motive, learned contended the deceased had petitioner’s proposal, allegedly prompted to commit the murder. On this basis, it was argued that the motive, being personal and emotional in nature, should be treated as a mitigating circumstance and the of death should be converted into imprisonment for life. The contention is absolutely misconceived untenable for the reason that such a motive does not soften the offence but serves to aggravate the same. The act was not the result of any sudden, grave and immediate provocation the evidence shows that the petitioner was aggrieved merely his marriage proposal was declined. Such a grievance cannot, by itself, be elevated to the status mitigation so as to dilute the normal penalty of death. This, in our view, is a result of ego-driven impulse of men in our society. provides us with the opportunity to investigate this malaise of ego-driven customs violence perpetrated by men against women in greater detail which will also help in understanding the nature of present case as having mitigating circumstance or not being one of aggravated nature.

We are aware that sentencing is a judicial discretion that must be exercised with consideration for the nature of the act, the manner of its commission, the vulnerability of the victim, and the social message that the criminal justice system is required to convey. The murder of an innocent girl solely she a marriage proposal is a grave offense. There are numerous victims of such offences around globe who are now suffering from life long trauma as a result. One such victim is Inteha Bibi, and the said trauma is explicitly depicted in her words as follows: “I have no life, I am traumatized, I have anxiety, sleep without medication. I am a human, and I have all the rights to get engaged and married to whoever I want. lama woman, not a toy, and I don’t want to be married to someone forcibly.” (Inteha Bibi, The Guardian, 19 December 2023)

It is a matter of profound shame to the conscience of any civilized society when a man fails to gain a woman’s affection and responds to her refusal with violence instead of acceptance. The sole reason he takes life is to appease his wounded ego, as he was unable to secure her hand and marry her. Marriage is a mutual, voluntary covenant that necessitates the free consent of both parties. However, in a variety of patriarchal systems, it is accepted that men have the exclusive right to select, demand, and enforce possession over a woman, irrespective of her wishes. A woman challenges suitor’s perceived ownership when she exercises fundamental right to say “no”. Under a patriarchal mindset, this rejection is taken by man a blow his “honor” (ghairat) results stalking, home invasion, acid violence, or femicide.

In the context of our country, practices of “ghag’ among others for example, is a manifestation of this mindset. Ghag (literally “cal? or “proclamation” in Pashto) is an archaic customary practice where a man unilaterally claims a woman as his bride without her or guardians’ consent. Historically, executed by firing gunshots outside the woman’s residence or making a public declaration. Ghag acts as an informal seal or taboo intimidating other perspective suitors away, holding the woman’s marital status hostage as if she is a territory, is now marked man. If she or her resists, the suitor frequently employs violence to enforce his claim. As a result, a woman may remain unmarried for years, or even decades, solely due to a declaration was never followed by a legal or religious ceremony, engagement, or marriage. Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Elimination of Custom of Ghag Act, 2013, was enacted by the provincial legislature in recognition of the severity of this issue. This Act declared ghag to be a cognizable, non-bailable, and non- compoundable criminal offense.

In the same vein, “swara” (also known vani or badal-e-sulh, “exchange for peace”) operates differently from ghag, despite the fact that both portrays situations where the decision to marry a woman is made by others for a purpose that is not in accordance with her own desires nor benefit. It involves a girl or young woman from a family that has committed an offense, such as homicide, given in marriage to a man from the victim’s family as a form of compensation through decision made by a jirga, serves a substitute for a criminal proceeding or financial compensation. The practice was criminalized through Criminal Law (Amendment) Act, 2004 and further solidified by Prevention of Anti-Women Practices Act, 2011.

Similarly, the custom of “watta-satta’” is another example where setting of marriage is at the cost of the bride’s well being. Watta-satta, which translates to “give-take”, is a reciprocal that is prevalent in our country involving a brother and sister from one family marry a sister and brother from another family in a single arrangement. Practices like Swara and Watta Satta rejects women as autonomous individuals and promote their commodification within patriarchal power structures. In Swara, an innocent woman sacrificed literally as compensation to settle a blood feud or criminal offense committed by a male relative, forcing her to bear the punitive weight of a crime she never committed. In Watta Satta, she is bartered as a biological surety or a living hostage ensuring any suffering inflicted on one side triggers retaliatory violence on the other.

Such practices are not limited to Pakistan mindset behind be caged by borders. Ala Kachuu (translating to grab and run) in Central Asia is a bride abduction practice where a man abducts a woman and takes her to his home, and his female relatives force a white headscarf on her to signify forced consent. Her or her family’s refusal results in social ostracization the pretense "honour" is already tainted. Similar practice is also found African region known as Telefa which is also forcible abduction young women to negotiate a post-facto settlement elders, using sexual violence or public abduction as a tool of coercion. While state laws formally criminalized these practices, the underlying motivation - that is the belief that a man can claim a woman by force or right - remains active in everyday social conduct.

A renowned anthropologist, Gayle Rubin gave the concept of the “traffic women” foundational essay, “The Traffic Women: Notes on the ‘Political Economy’ of Sex’, describing how women are treated as gifts, currency, or objects of exchange between men to build social and kinship ties. This elaborates the fact that for a very long time women have been treated by men across different regions as a commodity despite modernization of civilizations this deep- rooted believe is still existing in the minds of men which result in a woman’s will to be treated as subordinate to male entitlement. It is from this very -.otion of ownership the most extreme forms of violence emerge when a woman refuses to submit, chooses her own life, or asserts independence, is perceived not an exercise of equal human agency but as a challenge to an assumed entitlement over her. In such a mindset, she ceases to be regarded an equal human being and is instead reduced to a commodity that can be exchanged, bought, possessed, or when necessary, snatched.

The common thread unites all of the customs previously mentioned is that in this male-dominanted society having patriarchal customs traditions, a woman’s assent to her own marriage considered irrelevant. It is impossible to reconcile this mindset Islam, requires the woman’s free assent as a prerequisite for a valid nikah. Any adult person, either a man or a woman, is equally entitled to decide whether, when, and with whom they will marry. That entitlement is not a concession that her family, tribe, or society as a whole has granted to her. She possesses this privilege in her own right. There is no excuse for such behavior, regardless of whether it is committed in the name of honor, custom, injured pride, or emotions. It would also be pertinent to mention here that our country is party to Convention on Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination Against Women (CEDAW), Article 16 whereof obliges States to ensure a woman has the same right freely to choose a spouse and to enter into marriage only with her free and full consent. A domestic custom or such prevalent mindset that nullifies this choice by force cannot be permitted to survive under the guise of local practice. This discussion sheds light on what made the petitioner commit the said act of murdering a young female in cold blood. In the case at hand, the petitioner seems to be suffering from the mindset which led to beliefs that a woman is a commodity and it is the right of the suitor to have her, no possibility of refusal commodities express. This attempt woman’s lawful “provocation” or as a mitigating circumstance is a very absurd no human the right to deprive another human of their life just of refusing a marriage proposal. Accepting such an argument would constitute judicial endorsement of the notion a woman’s will is subordinate a man’s preference. Hence, in the light of above discussion, we have come to the conclusion the case at hand presents no mitigating circumstance, rather is a situation exhibiting a very grave and aggravated form of offence thereby strengthening non-applicability of the life expectancy principle.

For the foregoing reasons, we find that failed to point out any error apparent on the face of the record, or any otherwise falling within the narrow compass of this Court’s review jurisdiction Article Constitution. submissions advanced are, in substance, a request to reargue and reweigh matters, which this Court, sitting in review, cannot undertake. Accordingly, the review petition is dismissed and leave is refused. Announced in open Court at Islamabad on Approved for Reporting (Farrukh,SPS/ Tayyaba Munir, Law Clerk)
